extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters / patent attorneys / patent agents preparing patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing and drafting patent applications, including patentability thresholds, disclosure requirements, application parts, inventor interactions, timing/priority and filing procedure across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter / exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain subject matter is excluded from patentability in many countries, for example where prevention of commercial exploitation is necessary to protect order public or morality; diagnostic, therapeutic and surgical methods for the treatment of humans or animals; and plants and animals (other than microorganisms) and essentially biological processes (other than microbiological processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Products designed for use in diagnostic, therapeutic or surgical treatments are not excluded and may be patented (medical products, apparatus and devices). In the United States, methods of treatment are not excluded in law, but a patentee cannot enforce such a patent against a medical practitioner. Assess patent-eligibility in each jurisdiction before proceeding: if subject matter is ineligible, novelty/inventiveness are irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: In return for exclusive rights, patent holders must sufficiently disclose information about the invention so the public can learn about the invention and avoid reinventing it; disclosure also ensures patent scope is clearly communicated so others can avoid infringement or challenge the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure objectives: dissemination of technological information, preventing unjustified extension of rights to undisclosed subject matter, and clarity of claim scope. Failure to properly disclose at filing can make it impossible to add new subject matter later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support requirement (or written description requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be supported by the description (written description in the United States): there must be a basis in the description for the subject matter of every claim and claims must not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is supported unless there are well‑founded reasons to believe a person skilled in the art could not extend the teaching of the description to the whole field claimed. U.S. written description requires describing the claimed invention in sufficient detail that a skilled person would reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention at filing. See Modules IV–VII for practical drafting guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must disclose the invention clearly and completely so a person skilled in the art can make and use the claimed invention without undue burden (undue experimentation) or inventive effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent of disclosure needed depends on predictability of the art and breadth of claims: broader claims typically require more disclosure. Known/common tools or processes need not be described in detail, but novel aspects must be explicitly disclosed in an enabling manner. Chemical compounds typically require more detail (how to produce and technical effects) than improvements to well-known mechanical machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity requirement (definiteness requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be clear and concise and distinctly define the subject matter of the invention, using neither vague nor indefinite terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms in a claim are given their normal meaning in the relevant art; where needed, the drafter can include explicit definitions in the description to give special meaning. Description and drawings may be taken into account when interpreting claims. Draft claims with clarity so third parties can analyze what is and is not covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries an applicant must disclose at least one mode (example) of carrying out the claimed invention; in others (including the United States) the applicant must disclose the 'best' mode known to the inventor at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best mode requirement is based on equity to prevent inventors from withholding the best way while claiming protection. Note: in the United States, failure to disclose the best mode is not a ground for invalidation or unenforceability of a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be new (novel); prior art that discloses the same invention anticipates and destroys novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention was published (e.g., academic journal) before filing, many countries will reject the application. For novelty, single prior art references are examined for anticipation; novelty is distinct from inventive step/nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step (nonobviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must involve an inventive step (be nonobvious) over the prior art; lack of inventive step can be shown by combining prior art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed invention would have been obvious to a person skilled in the art given the prior art. This is conceptually distinct from novelty. Consider combination of references when evaluating inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability (utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be industrially applicable or useful; it must have some practical application or utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industrial applicability ensures the invention can be made or used in some industry. Note: an invention does not generally need to be superior to existing products or processes to meet utility. Utility/industrial applicability can be problematic for some chemical compounds and processes where demonstrating a practical use is difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess patent-eligibility before drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: You must first assess whether the invention is patent-eligible subject matter in the jurisdictions of interest; if not, a patent cannot be obtained even if novel and inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not invest drafting effort if subject matter is excluded in target jurisdictions. The manual's 'Professional tip' stresses early assessment of eligibility as essential to the drafting decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and time‑barring events (filing urgency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine how soon the application needs to be filed relative to events such as first attempted commercial exploitation, first export, first public disclosure, and other time bars in each jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the client/inventor about these events and verify facts yourself. File as quickly as possible because third parties may file similar applications or conduct disclosures that can defeat patentability. 'One day late is too late.' Document and docket critical dates; when filing in hard copy, save mail deposit receipts; when filing electronically, save confirmations to prove filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority claims (Paris Convention and PCT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants from Paris Convention or WTO member states can claim priority when filing subsequent applications in those territories within 12 months of the first application; PCT also allows priority claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valid priority means subsequent applications are not invalidated by actions between the priority date and the subsequent filing date. Docket the first application's filing date and check with the applicant before its first anniversary about foreign filing intentions. Determine special rules for countries not party to the Paris Convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional patent applications as placeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional patent application (U.S. context) must disclose the invention but need not include patent claims; it expires one year after filing and serves as a placeholder if a regular utility application is filed within one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provisional filings for urgent time bars when a full application cannot be prepared in time. After filing a provisional, create a complete folder and follow up with a full application within the year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining invention disclosures from inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Gather technical information and business context from inventors via invention disclosures, sketches, lab reports, prototypes, manuscripts, etc., and aim to have at least one meeting (in person, telephone or video) with inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review disclosure materials promptly and note technical and legal questions. Adapt and use invention disclosure forms (sample in Annex B) to legal requirements of jurisdictions. For some clients provide a blank form; for others conduct interviews. Professional tip: always negotiate fees with clients before incurring charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying patentable inventions (focus on concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: From disclosures/interviews, focus on the patentable inventions (the inventive concept) rather than prototypes or nonpatentable details; the drafter often articulates what constitutes the invention to be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore with the inventor the problem they solved in light of prior art to craft essential claim elements. Do not assume inventors know what is patentable; ask probing questions to identify novel and inventive aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the invention / core inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the invention well enough to define it by the fewest possible elements and to distinguish essential elements from nonessential ones, and to disclose all possibly patentable aspects and alternative embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask questions about alternatives and variations (e.g., could the surface be prepared any way other than burning?). Ensure at least one working embodiment is disclosed; if you add material to fill gaps, confirm accuracy with the inventor. Consider broadening by identifying alternative embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application must include the name(s) of the inventor(s); inventorship should reflect persons who made a creative contribution to the inventive concept (jurisdictional tests vary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify who truly qualifies as an inventor (creative contribution vs mere supervision, data collection, funding). Incorrect inventorship can lead to challenges such as fraud or misappropriation, possibly rendering a patent invalid or unenforceable. Check amendability rules in the target jurisdictions before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical parts of a patent application (content requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application typically includes a request (application form), a description, one or more claims, drawings (if necessary), and an abstract; sequence listings may be required for nucleotide/amino acid sequences and additional documents (power of attorney, inventor identity, entitlement, oath/declaration) vary by jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are the heart of a patent and often drafted first because the description content is partly dictated by the claims. Ensure all priority information and related application data are included either in the request form or an application data sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request (application form) content
rubrics_metrics.description: The request explicitly states the applicant seeks patent protection and is signed; request/application forms generally contain the title of the invention, the name and address of the applicant and representative, indication of the inventor, and priority claim information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include all priority/related application information either on the request form or in the application data sheet (e.g., CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATION in U.S. practice). Use patent office sample forms to ensure conformity to local requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description structure and content
rubrics_metrics.description: The description should disclose the invention sufficiently clearly and completely (so a skilled person can carry it out) and typically contains: title, technical field, background art, summary of the invention, brief explanation of drawings, and detailed examples/embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/embodiments play an important role in meeting support and enablement requirements. Format and section headings vary by jurisdiction; tailor the description accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims drafting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the scope of exclusive protection in terms of technical features; they are the legally operative part and must be clear, concise, and fully supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims in the proper formal claim format. Consider drafting claims first to guide the rest of the specification. Ensure claim words are given appropriate meanings and that claim scope is justified by the description and drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings purpose and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings provide visual support to describe the invention and facilitate understanding; they may include figures, tables, flow charts and diagrams, and a representative drawing is often placed on the front page of a published patent document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include drawings where necessary to understand the invention; ensure consistency with the description and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract is a short summary (digest) of the invention, limited to a certain number of words, typically including key features recited in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract aids patent searches and gives an overview of the invention. Keep within jurisdictional word-limits and ensure it reflects claim features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application format and additional documentary requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the five main parts are common, detailed format and additional documents (power of attorney, inventor identity, entitlement documents, oath/declaration, sequence listings for biological sequences) vary across national/regional laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the rules of each target territory for specific formatting and documentary requirements; use patent office sample forms where available (Common Application Format (CAF) noted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional filing practices and record-keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing by post, create a folder with a copy of everything sent including mail deposit receipt; when filing electronically, save/print the patent office confirmation to prove filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain contemporaneous records to prove filing date if the patent office misattributes receipt. Docket deadlines and follow up on priority dates well ahead of anniversaries. The manual emphasizes timely filing: 'One day late is too late.'
